propositions.text: Whether toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. exempting criminal responsibility.
propositions.quote: the Court must decide whether a toxic psychosis that results from a state of self‑induced intoxication caused by an accused person’s use of chemical drugs constitutes a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 of the Criminal Code

propositions.text: Review the scopes of insanity defence and self-induced intoxication defence generally.
propositions.quote: this case also gives the Court an opportunity to review the respective scopes of the insanity defence and the defence of self‑induced intoxication

paragraphs.summary: The Court must decide if toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. and review insanity and intoxication defences.

propositions.text: Appellant assaulted two individuals in psychotic state caused by drugs taken hours earlier, seriously injuring one.
propositions.quote: The appellant brutally assaulted two individuals while he was in a psychotic condition caused by chemical drugs he had taken a few hours earlier

propositions.text: Appellant convicted by Court of Québec on aggravated assault and assault charges.
propositions.quote: After being convicted by the Court of Québec on two counts of aggravated assault and assault

propositions.text: Appellant unsuccessfully appealed for not criminally responsible verdict due to mental disorder.
propositions.quote: the appellant tried unsuccessfully on appeal to obtain a verdict of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder

propositions.text: Appellant now appeals Quebec Court of Appeal judgment rejecting toxic psychosis as 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: With leave of this Court, the appellant is now appealing the judgment of the Quebec Court of Appeal, which rejected the argument that a toxic psychosis resulting from the voluntary consumption of drugs is a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant assaulted two people in drug-induced psychosis, was convicted, unsuccessfully appealed, and now appeals the Court of Appeal's rejection of his mental disorder defence.

propositions.text: Court finds Court of Appeal's judgment correct in law and would dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: I find that the judgment of the Court of Appeal is correct in law. I would therefore dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Court of Appeal's judgment legally correct and would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: Appellant and acquaintance smoked marijuana and took amphetamines on October 23, 2005, then traveled intoxicated by bus to Mont-Joli.
propositions.quote: the appellant, Tommy Bouchard‑Lebrun, and a long‑time acquaintance of his, Yohann Schmouth, had smoked marijuana and taken amphetamines during the day on October 23, 2005. In the evening, they decided to go to Amqui so the appellant could visit his parents. They took the bus from Rivière‑du‑Loup, where the appellant lived, to the last stop in Mont‑Joli. They were still intoxicated when they got on the bus.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellant and acquaintance used drugs on October 23 and traveled intoxicated by bus to Mont-Joli.

propositions.text: Appellant and friend hitchhiked to Amqui; no signs of intoxication were apparent during car trip with acquaintance Gilles Tremblay.
propositions.quote: At about 1:30 a.m., Gilles Tremblay, an old acquaintance of the appellant’s family, picked them up in his car. At that time, no signs of intoxication were apparent from the appellant’s behaviour.

propositions.text: Witnesses confirmed appellant was 'OK' again near Val-Brillant; drugs taken earlier had ceased effect before arrival in Amqui.
propositions.quote: His statements confirmed Mr. Schmouth’s testimony that the appellant was [translation] “OK” again when they were around Val‑Brillant, a municipality about 15 kilometres from Amqui. Therefore, it seems that the drugs taken by the appellant during the day on October 23 had ceased to have effect before he arrived in Amqui with Mr. Schmouth.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant showed no intoxication signs during car trip and drugs taken earlier had ceased effect before Amqui.

propositions.text: In Amqui, appellant and friend took ecstasy pills and later decided to attack Dany Lévesque for wearing an 'upside-down cross'.
propositions.quote: In Amqui, the two young men purchased ecstasy pills of a type known as “poire bleue”, which they took during the night on October 24. During the hours that followed, the appellant and Mr. Schmouth decided to go and beat up Dany Lévesque, who was known as “Pee‑Wee”, for the real or imagined reason that he wore an [translation] “upside‑down cross” around his neck.

propositions.text: Appellant and friend illegally entered Lévesque's building and brutally attacked him by punching and kicking.
propositions.quote: Around 5:00 a.m., the appellant and Mr. Schmouth illegally entered the building where Mr. Lévesque lived. ... the latter two then brutally attacked Mr. Lévesque by punching and kicking him many times.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellant and friend took ecstasy, then attacked Lévesque for wearing an upside-down cross.

propositions.text: Mr. Dumas tried to intervene; appellant violently threw him down stairs and stomped on his head, causing lifelong disability.
propositions.quote: Mr. Dumas saw that Mr. Lévesque could not defend himself against his two attackers and tried to intervene. The appellant grabbed him and threw him violently down the stairs. ... The assault left Mr. Dumas disabled, and he will have to spend the rest of his life in a hospital.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant violently assaulted Mr. Dumas, causing lifelong disability.

propositions.text: At assault time, appellant was highly intoxicated from 'poire bleue' pill, causing dissociation from reality and 'being on another planet'.
propositions.quote: At the time of the assault, the appellant was highly intoxicated because of the effects of the “poire bleue” pill he had taken a few hours earlier. ... it caused a complete dissociation between the appellant’s subjective perceptions and the objective reality. To put it bluntly, he was [translation] “on another planet”.

propositions.text: Two trial witnesses said appellant 'started acting weird' and was 'completely out of it' after taking the pill.
propositions.quote: Two witnesses at the trial stated that he [translation] “started acting weird” and was “completely out of it” after taking the “poire bleue” pill.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant was highly intoxicated and dissociated after taking the pill, with witnesses noting odd behavior.

propositions.text: Appellant experienced religious delirium, obsessed with upside-down cross, made absurd religious statements during attack.
propositions.quote: In actual fact, the appellant experienced an episode that might be described as religious delirium in light of its symptoms. ... he became obsessed with the “upside‑down cross” supposedly worn by Mr. Lévesque. During the attack, he made statements of a religious nature that, although coherent, were basically absurd.

propositions.text: Appellant asked victims if they believed in him, blessed Mr. Dumas’s spouse, then left calmly as if nothing happened.
propositions.quote: At one point, he raised his arms in the air and asked the victims and the helpless witnesses to the attack whether they believed in him. ... he blessed Mr. Dumas’s spouse by making the sign of the cross on her forehead. ... he then left the scene very calmly as if nothing had just happened.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant had religious delirium, made absurd statements, blessed a witness, then left calmly.

propositions.text: It is undisputed appellant was in serious psychotic condition at offences time, which diminished by October 28, 2005.
propositions.quote: It has never been in dispute, in any of the courts, that the appellant was in a serious psychotic condition at the time of the offences and that the effects of that condition diminished gradually until they disappeared on October 28, 2005.

propositions.text: The essential issue is how the psychosis affects appellant’s criminal responsibility.
propositions.quote: The essential issue in this appeal is instead how that psychosis affects the appellant’s criminal responsibility.

propositions.text: Appellant had no prior psychotic episodes, no underlying mental disease, no addiction; described as occasional drug user without abuse evidence.
propositions.quote: the appellant had never experienced a psychotic episode such as this prior to the incidents in question. He had no underlying disease of the mind, nor was he addicted to a particular substance. ... the evidence does not establish that he “abused” drugs

paragraphs.summary: The court notes undisputed serious psychosis at offence time, no prior episodes or addiction, and issue is effect on responsibility.

propositions.text: Appellant charged with aggravated assault and breaking and entering offences; pleaded not guilty.
propositions.quote: As a result of these incidents, the appellant was charged with committing aggravated assault ... and with breaking and entering ... He pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellant was charged with assault and breaking and entering, and pleaded not guilty.

propositions.text: At trial, appellant raised defence of psychotic condition induced by friend’s spiritual influence, claiming it prevented judgment on drug effects.
propositions.quote: he claimed that, at the time, he had been under the effects of a psychotic condition induced by Mr. Schmouth’s spiritual influence. The defence’s position was that this psychotic condition had prevented the appellant from exercising judgment to assess what impact his drug‑taking ... might have

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge reports appellant’s defence was psychosis from friend’s spiritual influence impairing judgment on drug effects.

propositions.text: Two psychiatrists agreed appellant was severely psychotic and incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at offence time.
propositions.quote: They were in agreement that the appellant had been suffering from [translation] “a severe psychosis that made him incapable of distinguishing right from wrong”

propositions.text: Defence expert said psychosis mainly from mystical influence of friend; appellant’s drug use influenced by friend’s control.
propositions.quote: Dr. Roger Turmel, the defence’s expert, stated that the appellant’s psychosis had resulted mainly from [translation] “the mystical atmosphere” into which he had been plunged by Mr. Schmouth. ... “even Mr. [Bouchard‑]Lebrun’s decision to take drugs was not made freely but was influenced in a way by the control his friend exerted over him”

propositions.text: Crown expert disagreed, said conditions for psychosis from third party influence not present; psychosis was toxic from substance use.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s expert disagreed with this. ... He concluded instead that, at the material time, the appellant had been suffering from toxic psychosis, that is, psychosis caused by the consumption of toxic substances

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge reports experts agreed on severe psychosis but disagreed on origin: mystical influence or toxic psychosis.

propositions.text: Judge Decoste accepted Crown expert’s opinion that appellant had toxic psychosis at offence time.
propositions.quote: Judge Decoste accepted Dr. Faucher’s opinion and found that the appellant had been suffering from toxic psychosis at the time he committed the offences

propositions.text: Appellant acquitted on breaking and entering counts due to extreme intoxication, convicted on aggravated assault counts referring to s. 33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: because of that state of extreme intoxication, the appellant had to be acquitted on the counts of breaking and entering ... He then convicted the appellant on the counts of aggravated assault ... referring for that purpose to s. 33.1 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Judge Decoste found toxic psychosis, acquitted appellant on breaking and entering, convicted on assault under s. 33.1.

propositions.text: Judge Decoste sentenced appellant to five years for aggravated assault and three months concurrent for common assault.
propositions.quote: Judge Decoste sentenced the appellant to imprisonment for five years for the offence of aggravated assault and three months concurrent for that of common assault.

paragraphs.summary: Judge Decoste sentenced appellant to five years for aggravated assault and three months concurrent for common assault.

propositions.text: On appeal, appellant conceded toxic psychosis but argued mental disorder defence should apply as he was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong.
propositions.quote: he no longer claimed that his psychotic condition had resulted from Mr. Schmouth’s spiritual influence. After conceding that he had acted under the influence of a toxic psychosis, he instead argued that the defence of mental disorder should have been applicable as a result of this condition, since the evidence at trial showed that he had been incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at the material time

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues on appeal that toxic psychosis was a mental disorder defence as he was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong.

propositions.text: Appellant argued trial judge confused insanity defence under s.16 with self-induced intoxication defence under s.33.1 and asked Court of Appeal to apply s.16 defence.
propositions.quote: In general terms, the appellant argued that the trial judge had confused the insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. with the defence of self‑induced intoxication under s. 33.1 Cr. C. He therefore asked the Court of Appeal to disregard s. 33.1 and find that he was not criminally responsible on the basis that his toxic psychosis ... was a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues trial judge confused insanity and intoxication defences and asks Court of Appeal to apply s.16 mental disorder defence.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal disagreed that psychotic condition was unforeseeable, citing expert testimony on likelihood of psychosis from PCP and amphetamines.
propositions.quote: Thibault J.A., writing for the court, began by expressing disagreement with the premise on which they were based, namely that the development of a psychotic condition was [translation] “unforeseeable” in this case. She noted that, on the contrary, Dr. Faucher’s testimony had proved that 50 percent of PCP users and 13 percent of amphetamine users were likely to develop such a condition

propositions.text: Appellant seemed to be among those likely to develop psychosis, as effects lasted as long as intoxication lasted.
propositions.quote: She added that the appellant seemed to be one of those people, since the effects of his psychosis had lasted as long as he had remained intoxicated

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal found psychosis was foreseeable and appellant was likely to develop it, lasting as long as intoxication.

propositions.text: Defence of self-induced intoxication is available in extreme cases for general intent offences, limited by s.33.1 to non-violent offences.
propositions.quote: according to the line of authority based on R. v. Daviault, ... the defence of self‑induced intoxication was available in extreme cases to accused persons charged with general intent offences. She added that the enactment by Parliament of s. 33.1 Cr. C. had limited this defence to non‑violent offences.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal states self-induced intoxication defence is limited by s.33.1 to non-violent offences.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal acknowledged insanity defence applies to underlying mental disorder worsened by drug use.
propositions.quote: she acknowledged that the courts had held that the defence was available to an accused person suffering from an underlying mental disorder whose mental condition had [translation] “deteriorated even more” as a result of drug use

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held transitory psychosis from drug use is not a 'disease of the mind' under ss. 2 and 16 Cr. C., citing Cooper v. The Queen.
propositions.quote: she pointed out that this Court had clearly held in Cooper v. The Queen, ... that transitory psychosis induced by drug use cannot be considered a “disease of the mind” within the meaning of ss. 2 and 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held appellant’s insanity defence under s.16 could not succeed due to psychotic condition being drug-induced.
propositions.quote: She accordingly held that because of the appellant’s psychotic condition at the time he assaulted his victims, his insanity defence under s. 16 of the Criminal Code could not succeed.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal held transitory drug-induced psychosis is not mental disorder defence and appellant’s insanity defence failed.

propositions.text: Appellant had no underlying disease of the mind and became sane after effects of 'poire bleue' passed
propositions.quote: the appellant had no underlying disease of the mind and had become perfectly sane again once the effects of the “poire bleue” had passed

propositions.text: Appellant's argument was an attempt to circumvent Parliament's intent to preclude self-induced intoxication defence
propositions.quote: the appellant’s argument was an attempt to circumvent Parliament’s intent by making it possible for an accused person to plead self‑induced intoxication to avoid criminal liability

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found appellant had no underlying mental disease and his argument tried to circumvent Parliament's intent, per Thibault J.A.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal dismissed appeal against sentence as sentences were harsh but not unreasonable
propositions.quote: the sentences imposed by the trial judge, though harsh, were not unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal against sentence, finding the sentences harsh but reasonable.

propositions.text: Does s. 33.1 Cr. C. limit the scope of the defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder in s. 16 Cr. C.?
propositions.quote: Does s. 33.1 Cr. C. limit the scope of the defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder provided for in s. 16 Cr. C.?

propositions.text: Can toxic psychosis caused by self-induced intoxication be a 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C.?
propositions.quote: Can a toxic psychosis whose symptoms are caused by a state of self‑induced intoxication be a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.?

paragraphs.summary: The appeal raises issues about s. 33.1 Cr. C.'s limitation on s. 16 defence and whether toxic psychosis from intoxication is a 'mental disorder'.

propositions.text: Appellant concedes toxic psychosis resulted exclusively from self-induced intoxication on October 24, 2005
propositions.quote: the evidence in the record shows that his toxic psychosis resulted exclusively from his state of self‑induced intoxication the night of October 24, 2005

propositions.text: Appellant disagrees courts failed to consider predisposition but does not argue intoxication triggered latent disease
propositions.quote: he is not specifically submitting that they erred in rejecting the argument that his intoxication had triggered a latent disease of the mind

paragraphs.summary: Appellant admits toxic psychosis was from self-induced intoxication and does not argue intoxication triggered latent disease.

propositions.text: Appellant argues a single intoxication episode causing abnormal effects like psychosis can be a 'mental disorder' under s. 16
propositions.quote: a single episode of intoxication can be a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. if it produces abnormal effects on the accused, such as psychotic symptoms

propositions.text: Appellant's syllogism: toxic psychosis affects only vulnerable psyches, so it must be a legal mental disorder
propositions.quote: since toxic psychosis is an abnormal effect of intoxication, it necessarily affects only those whose psyches are particularly fragile or vulnerable

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues toxic psychosis from intoxication is a legal mental disorder because it affects only vulnerable individuals.

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis results from underlying mental disease but relies on general argument, not personal facts
propositions.quote: he relies on an argument of general application... any toxic psychosis... must be considered a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Appellant's premise: intoxication cannot be the real cause of toxic psychosis; it must originate in pre-existing condition
propositions.quote: intoxication can never be the real or underlying cause of toxic psychosis and that toxic psychosis must originate in a pre‑existing mental condition

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues generally that toxic psychosis must be a mental disorder from pre-existing condition, not intoxication.

propositions.text: Appellant contends psychotic condition legally cannot be mere intoxication and Court of Appeal confused defences
propositions.quote: a person in a psychotic condition should never, from a legal standpoint, be considered merely to be intoxicated

propositions.text: Appellant argues s. 33.1 Cr. C. was wrongly applied and limits mental disorder defence scope
propositions.quote: [h]is submission would have the effect of rendering s. 33.1 Cr. C. meaningless and [disregarding] the clearly expressed legislative intent

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues psychosis is not mere intoxication and s. 33.1 Cr. C. wrongly limits mental disorder defence.

propositions.text: Appellant says s. 33.1 Cr. C. endorses Daviault dissent that self-induced intoxication defence unavailable for general intent offences
propositions.quote: Parliament... endorsed the position taken by the dissenting judges in Daviault that... the defence of self‑induced intoxication should not be available in the case of a general intent offence

propositions.text: Appellant submits dissent balanced punishing voluntary intoxication but protecting those lacking mental capacity
propositions.quote: the dissent in Daviault struck a judicious balance and gave effect to society’s wish to punish reprehensible acts... but not to punish those who lack the mental capacity

propositions.text: Appellant cites Sopinka J. dissent that drug-induced mental illness affects fragile, vulnerable individuals
propositions.quote: those who become mentally ill as a result of drug use are fragile and vulnerable individuals who are predisposed to mental disorders

propositions.text: Appellant raises no constitutional challenge to s. 33.1 Cr. C., only interpretation and application
propositions.quote: appellant raises no arguments regarding the constitutionality of s. 33.1 Cr. C., which means that only the interpretation and application of that provision are in issue

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues s. 33.1 Cr. C. endorses Daviault dissent balancing punishment and protection, raising no constitutional issues.

propositions.text: Three seminal cases led to enactment of s. 33.1 Cr. C., starting with House of Lords decision in DPP v. Beard
propositions.quote: There are three seminal cases in this regard. The first is the decision of the House of Lords in Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard

propositions.text: Beard set out three rules about intoxication and insanity defence as summarized in R. v. Daley
propositions.quote: Lord Birkenhead set out the following three rules (as summarized by Bastarache J. in R. v. Daley, 2007 SCC 53, at para. 34): (1) intoxication could be a ground for insanity defence if it produced disease of the mind; (2) evidence of drunkenness affecting specific intent should be considered; (3) drunkenness short of incapacity does not rebut presumption of intent

paragraphs.summary: Court summarizes seminal cases leading to s. 33.1 Cr. C., starting with Beard's three rules on intoxication and insanity defence.

propositions.text: Beard principle: intoxication can be defence for specific intent offences, subject to Robinson qualification
propositions.quote: intoxication can be raised as a defence in respect of a specific intent offence in certain circumstances

propositions.text: Robinson held Beard's third rule violated Charter and replaced it with intoxication defence if accused lacked actual specific intent
propositions.quote: Robinson... held that the third of the rules from Beard... violated ss. 7 and 11 (d) of the Canadian Charter... intoxication can be a defence if it prevented the accused from forming the actual specific intent

paragraphs.summary: Beard allows intoxication defence for specific intent offences, modified by Robinson to require lack of actual specific intent.

propositions.text: Since Beard, intoxication defence applies to specific intent offences; Leary held self-induced intoxication cannot raise doubt for general intent offences
propositions.quote: Since Beard... intoxication defence to acquit specific intent offences; Leary held self‑induced intoxication cannot raise doubt for general intent offences

propositions.text: Leary established recklessness in becoming intoxicated can satisfy fault for general intent offences
propositions.quote: Leary... established the principle that the recklessness shown by an accused in becoming voluntarily intoxicated can constitute the fault element needed to find that a general intent offence has been committed

paragraphs.summary: Leary held self-induced intoxication cannot raise doubt for general intent offences; recklessness suffices for fault.

propositions.text: Daviault majority held Leary rule violated Charter and allowed intoxication akin to automatism or insanity to raise reasonable doubt for general intent offences
propositions.quote: Daviault... majority held that the “substituted mens rea” rule from Leary was contrary to ss. 7 and 11 (d) of the Charter... accused in a “state akin to automatism or insanity” could raise reasonable doubt

paragraphs.summary: Daviault majority rejected Leary, allowing intoxication akin to automatism or insanity to raise reasonable doubt for general intent offences.

propositions.text: Sopinka J. dissented in Daviault, supporting Leary rule and emphasizing society's right to punish voluntary intoxication
propositions.quote: Sopinka J. wrote a strong dissent... no reason to abandon the Leary rule... society’s right “to punish those who of their own free will render themselves so intoxicated”

paragraphs.summary: Sopinka J. dissented in Daviault, supporting Leary and society's right to punish voluntary intoxication.

propositions.text: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. to prevent intoxication defence for general intent violent crimes
propositions.quote: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. to ensure that “intoxication may never be used as a defence against general intent violent crimes such as sexual assault and assault”

propositions.text: s. 33.1 Cr. C. prohibits defence of self-induced intoxication for offences involving bodily integrity interference
propositions.quote: 33.1 (1) It is not a defence... that the accused, by reason of self‑induced intoxication, lacked the general intent... where the accused departed markedly from the standard of care...

paragraphs.summary: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. to bar intoxication defence for general intent violent crimes involving bodily integrity.

propositions.text: Appellant argues Parliament implicitly endorsed Sopinka J.'s dissent by enacting s. 33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: appellant can reasonably argue that Parliament implicitly endorsed Sopinka J.’s dissent in Daviault by enacting s. 33.1 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Enactment of s. 33.1 Cr. C. limited majority's rule in Daviault; did not revive Leary rule
propositions.quote: It did not actually codify the position taken by the dissenting judges in Daviault; rather, it limited the scope of the rule stated by the majority

propositions.text: Daviault principles remain law except for s. 33.1 Cr. C. restriction; appellant's acquittal on property charges shows this
propositions.quote: principles set out in Daviault still represent the state of the law in Canada, subject... to the significant restriction set out in s. 33.1 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues s. 33.1 Cr. C. endorses dissent, but Court finds it limits Daviault majority rule; Daviault still law except s. 33.1.

propositions.text: s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not limit scope of s. 16 Cr. C.; intoxication and insanity are distinct legal concepts with different principles
propositions.quote: s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not be interpreted so as to limit the scope of s. 16 Cr. C. Intoxication and insanity are two distinct legal concepts

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not limit s. 16 Cr. C.; intoxication and insanity are distinct defences.

propositions.text: Application of s. 16 Cr. C. and s. 33.1 Cr. C. are mutually exclusive; intoxication precludes disease of mind finding
propositions.quote: For s. 33.1 Cr. C. to apply... absence of intent or voluntariness would preclude a finding that the incapacity was caused by a disease of the mind

propositions.text: If accused was intoxicated but incapable due to mental disorder, s. 33.1 Cr. C. does not apply
propositions.quote: the fact that an accused was intoxicated... cannot support a finding that s. 33.1 Cr. C. applies if the accused establishes incapacity by mental disorder

paragraphs.summary: Court states s. 16 and s. 33.1 Cr. C. defences are mutually exclusive; intoxication excludes disease of mind finding.

propositions.text: Court must identify source of psychosis—self-induced intoxication or disease of mind—to determine criminal responsibility
propositions.quote: the problem the court faces is to identify a specific source for his or her mental condition... self‑induced intoxication or a disease of the mind

propositions.text: Identification is difficult when mental health was precarious before intoxication and psychosis emerged during intoxication
propositions.quote: all the more difficult... mental health... precarious prior... psychosis emerged while... highly intoxicated

propositions.text: Source identification determines whether accused is criminally responsible
propositions.quote: this identification of the source of the psychosis plays a key role, since it will ultimately determine whether the accused will be held criminally responsible

paragraphs.summary: Court explains identifying psychosis source is key to criminal responsibility, especially with prior mental health issues.

propositions.text: Legal concept of 'disease of the mind' excludes self-induced intoxication and transitory mental states
propositions.quote: “disease of the mind” embraces any illness... impairing the mind, excluding... self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs, as well as transitory mental states

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Cooper defining 'disease of the mind' excluding self-induced intoxication and transitory states.

propositions.text: Court must first analyze insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. before considering s. 33.1 Cr. C. applicability
propositions.quote: court must not begin its analysis by considering whether the mental condition... is covered by s. 33.1 Cr. C.... must consider... insanity defence

propositions.text: Legal characterization under s. 16 Cr. C. must not depend on causation interpretation in s. 33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: legal characterization exercise required by s. 16 Cr. C. would depend on the interpretation of the concept of causation in issue in s. 33.1 Cr. C

paragraphs.summary: Court holds analysis must start with s. 16 insanity defence before s. 33.1 intoxication defence; legal characterization must not depend on s. 33.1 causation.

propositions.text: These observations delineate the scopes of ss. 16 and 33.1 Cr. C. but do not dispose of the appellant's main argument on insanity defence content.
propositions.quote: These observations, which are necessary to broadly delineate the respective scopes of ss. 16 and 33.1 Cr. C., do not dispose of the appellant’s main argument regarding the actual content of the insanity defence.

propositions.text: Cooper’s exclusion of self-induced states applies only to normal intoxication effects, not abnormal effects like toxic psychosis.
propositions.quote: The appellant submits that Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs” applies only to the normal effects of intoxication (transcript, at p. 20).

propositions.text: The issue is whether toxic psychosis from intoxication is a mental disorder under s. 16 Cr. C. or excluded by Cooper.
propositions.quote: In this context, what remains to be determined is whether a toxic psychosis that results exclusively from a state of intoxication, which the appellant views as an “abnormal effect” of intoxication, constitutes a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. or is excluded by Cooper.

paragraphs.summary: The court says these observations do not resolve the appellant's argument that toxic psychosis from intoxication is a mental disorder under s.16 or excluded by Cooper.

propositions.text: It is necessary to examine Cooper’s exclusion of self-induced states from s. 16 Cr. C.; the court will return to this later.
propositions.quote: It is therefore necessary to take a closer look at the scope of Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs” from the ambit of s. 16 Cr. C. I will come back to this later.

propositions.text: The appellant criticizes the Court of Appeal’s position on ss. 16 and 33.1 interplay as incorrect.
propositions.quote: the appellant’s criticism of the Court of Appeal’s position on the interplay between ss. 16 and 33.1 Cr. C. is unfounded.

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. did not infer s. 33.1 limits s. 16 defence; she said no overlap is possible and psychosis from drug consumption excludes s. 16 application.
propositions.quote: Thibault J.A. did not infer that s. 33.1 Cr. C. limits the scope of the defence of mental disorder provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. She stated clearly that no overlap is possible in the application of these provisions and simply concluded that, as the law stands in Canada, [translation] “an accused suffering from a psychosis caused by the consumption of drugs in circumstances analogous to the ones in the case before us” cannot be found to have a disease of the mind for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. (para. 77).

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. noted appellant was intoxicated and said appellant’s argument was an indirect way to avoid s. 33.1 application.
propositions.quote: After noting that the appellant had to be considered from a legal standpoint to have been intoxicated at the material time, Thibault J.A. added that the appellant’s argument was an indirect way to avoid the application of s. 33.1 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court says the appellant's criticism of the Court of Appeal is unfounded; Thibault J.A. found no overlap between ss.16 and 33.1 and excluded s.16 for drug-induced psychosis.

propositions.text: The fundamental issue is whether the Court of Appeal erred in applying s. 33.1 Cr. C. instead of s. 16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: Thus, the fundamental issue at this point is whether the Court of Appeal erred in law in holding that s. 33.1 Cr. C. was applicable in this case rather than s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: To resolve this, the court must consider legal principles and policy underlying s. 16 Cr. C. defence.
propositions.quote: To resolve it, I must consider the legal principles and judicial policy considerations that underlie the interpretation and application of the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the key issue is whether the Court of Appeal erred applying s.33.1 instead of s.16, requiring review of s.16 legal principles and policy.

propositions.text: The defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder addresses legitimate concerns in a democratic society.
propositions.quote: The defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder, which Parliament codified in s. 16 Cr. C., addresses concerns that are very legitimate in a democratic society.

propositions.text: Proper application of this defence protects the criminal justice system's integrity and collective interest in fundamental principles.
propositions.quote: a verdict of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder protects the integrity of our country’s criminal justice system and the collective interest in ensuring respect for its fundamental principles.

propositions.text: Reviewing fundamental criminal law principles confirms the defence's importance in Canadian law.
propositions.quote: A review of the fundamental principles of criminal law that underlie the defence of mental disorder confirms the importance of this defence in Canadian criminal law.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the mental disorder defence addresses legitimate concerns and protects the criminal justice system's integrity and fundamental principles.

propositions.text: Criminal responsibility requires commission of a voluntary act, a fundamental common law principle.
propositions.quote: According to a traditional fundamental principle of the common law, criminal responsibility can result only from the commission of a voluntary act.

propositions.text: It is unfair to impose criminal responsibility on one who did not voluntarily commit the offence.
propositions.quote: it would be unfair in a democratic society to impose the consequences and stigma of criminal responsibility on an accused who did not voluntarily commit an act that constitutes a criminal offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states criminal responsibility requires a voluntary act; imposing it on involuntary acts is unfair in a democratic society.

propositions.text: An act is voluntary if it is the product of the accused's free will, a willing mind making a definite choice.
propositions.quote: For an act to be considered voluntary in the criminal law, it must be the product of the accused person’s free will. As Taschereau J. stated in R. v. King, [1962] S.C.R. 746, “there can be no actus reus unless it is the result of a willing mind at liberty to make a definite choice or decision, or in other words, there must be a willpower to do an act whether the accused knew or not that it was prohibited by law” (p. 749).

propositions.text: Dickson J.'s dissent in Rabey, endorsed in Parks, holds no one is criminally responsible for involuntary acts.
propositions.quote: no one can be found criminally responsible for an involuntary act (see Dickson J.’s dissenting reasons in Rabey v. The Queen, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 513, which were endorsed on this point in R. v. Parks, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 871).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains voluntary acts require free will and willing mind; involuntary acts do not attract criminal responsibility per precedent.

propositions.text: Will is expressed by conscious control over body; voluntariness relates to physical and moral control over actions.
propositions.quote: An individual’s will is expressed through conscious control exerted by the individual over his or her body (Perka v. The Queen, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 232, at p. 249). The control may be physical, in which case voluntariness relates to the muscle movements of a person exerting physical control over his or her body. The exercise of a person’s will may also involve moral control over actions the person wants to take, in which case a voluntary act is a carefully thought out act that is performed freely by an individual with at least a minimum level of intelligence (see H. Parent, Responsabilité pénale et troubles mentaux: Histoire de la folie en droit pénal français, anglais et canadien (1999), at pp. 266‑71).

propositions.text: Will is also a product of reason, involving moral control and intelligence.
propositions.quote: Will is also a product of reason.

paragraphs.summary: The court states will is conscious control over body and reason, involving physical and moral control over actions.

propositions.text: Voluntary act's moral dimension reflects criminal law's view of individuals as autonomous, rational beings.
propositions.quote: The moral dimension of the voluntary act, which this Court recognized in Perka, thus reflects the idea that the criminal law views individuals as autonomous and rational beings.

propositions.text: Autonomy and reason are cornerstones of criminal responsibility principles (Alexander and Ferzan).
propositions.quote: Indeed, this idea can be seen as the cornerstone of the principles governing the attribution of criminal responsibility (L. Alexander and K. K. Ferzan with contributions by S. J. Morse, Crime and Culpability: A Theory of Criminal Law (2009), at p. 155).

propositions.text: Criminal responsibility requires true choice or free will, respecting autonomy and reason (Ruzic).
propositions.quote: When considered from this perspective, human behaviour will trigger criminal responsibility only if it results from a “true choice” or from the person’s “free will”. This principle signals the importance of autonomy and reason in the system of criminal responsibility. As the Court noted in R. v. Ruzic, 2001 SCC 24, [2001] 1 S.C.R. 687: The treatment of criminal offenders as rational, autonomous and choosing agents is a fundamental organizing principle of our criminal law. Its importance is reflected not only in the requirement that an act must be voluntary, but also in the condition that a wrongful act must be intentional to ground a conviction. . . . Like voluntariness, the requirement of a guilty mind is rooted in respect for individual autonomy and free will and acknowledges the importance of those values to a free and democratic society . . . . Criminal liability also depends on the capacity to choose — the ability to reason right from wrong. [Emphasis added; citation omitted; para. 45.]

paragraphs.summary: The court explains voluntary acts reflect autonomy and reason, fundamental to criminal responsibility, citing Ruzic and legal theory.

propositions.text: Criminal law presumes individuals can distinguish right from wrong and are autonomous and rational.
propositions.quote: This essential basis for attributing criminal responsibility thus gives rise to a presumption that each individual can distinguish right from wrong. The criminal law relies on a presumption that every person is an autonomous and rational being whose acts and omissions can attract liability.

propositions.text: This presumption is rebuttable by proof the accused lacked autonomy or rationality at the material time.
propositions.quote: This presumption is not absolute, however: it can be rebutted by proving that the accused did not at the material time have the level of autonomy or rationality required to attract criminal liability.

propositions.text: Criminal responsibility requires a discerning moral agent capable of choosing right from wrong (Chaulk).
propositions.quote: there is “a fundamental conviction that criminal responsibility is appropriate only where the actor is a discerning moral agent, capable of making choices between right and wrong” (R. v. Chaulk, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1303, at p. 1397).

propositions.text: Only voluntary conduct should attract criminal liability, a principle of fundamental justice (Ruzic).
propositions.quote: In Ruzic, the Court recognized the existence of a principle of fundamental justice that “only voluntary conduct — behaviour that is the product of a free will and controlled body, unhindered by external constraints — should attract the penalty and stigma of criminal liability” (para. 47).

paragraphs.summary: The court states criminal law presumes autonomy and rationality but allows rebuttal; only voluntary conduct attracts liability per fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Insanity is an exception to the presumption of autonomy and rationality in criminal law.
propositions.quote: Insanity is an exception to the general criminal law principle that an accused is deemed to be autonomous and rational.

propositions.text: A person with a mental disorder under s.16 Cr. C. cannot appreciate their acts' nature or know they are wrong.
propositions.quote: A person suffering from a mental disorder within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. is not considered to be capable of appreciating the nature of his or her acts or understanding that they are inherently wrong.

propositions.text: Insanity provisions exempt from criminal liability due to incapacity for criminal intent (Chaulk).
propositions.quote: the insanity provisions of the Criminal Code “operate, at the most fundamental level, as an exemption from criminal liability which is predicated on an incapacity for criminal intent” (p. 1321 (emphasis deleted)).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains insanity is an exception to autonomy presumption, exempting from liability due to incapacity for criminal intent under s.16.

propositions.text: An insane person is incapable of morally voluntary conduct; their actions are not products of free will.
propositions.quote: The logic of Ruzic is that it can also be said that an insane person is incapable of morally voluntary conduct. The person’s actions are not actually the product of his or her free will.

propositions.text: It is consistent with fundamental justice that a person covered by s.16 Cr. C. is not criminally responsible.
propositions.quote: It is therefore consistent with the principles of fundamental justice for a person whose mental condition at the relevant time is covered by s. 16 Cr. C. not to be criminally responsible under Canadian law.

propositions.text: Convicting involuntary actors undermines criminal law foundations and judicial integrity.
propositions.quote: Convicting a person who acted involuntarily would undermine the foundations of the criminal law and the integrity of the judicial system.

paragraphs.summary: The court states insane persons lack moral voluntariness; convicting them undermines justice, so s.16 exempts them from responsibility.

propositions.text: The mental disorder defence leads to a verdict of not criminally responsible, triggering an administrative process.
propositions.quote: However, the defence of mental disorder remains unique. It does not result in acquittal of the accused, but instead leads to a verdict of not criminally responsible.

propositions.text: This process assesses public safety threat and provides care, balancing treatment and protection interests.
propositions.quote: That verdict triggers an administrative process whose purpose is to determine whether the accused is a significant threat to the safety of the public, to take any necessary action to control that threat and, if necessary, to provide the accused with appropriate care.

propositions.text: The verdict ensures morally innocent offenders are treated, not punished, while protecting the public.
propositions.quote: A verdict of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder thus gives effect to society’s interest in ensuring that morally innocent offenders are treated rather than punished, while protecting the public as fully as possible.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the mental disorder defence results in a not criminally responsible verdict, triggering treatment and public safety processes.

propositions.text: An accused found not criminally responsible is subject to Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code scheme.
propositions.quote: An accused who is found not criminally responsible becomes subject to the scheme established in Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Part XX.1 replaced common law regime after Swain held automatic detention violated s.7 Charter right to liberty.
propositions.quote: Parliament adopted the current scheme after this Court had held in R. v. Swain, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 933, that a Criminal Code provision requiring the automatic and indeterminate detention of an accused found not criminally responsible violated the right to liberty guaranteed by s. 7 of the Charter .

propositions.text: Winko explained Part XX.1 emphasizes individualized assessment and treatment, balancing public protection and fairness.
propositions.quote: In Winko v. British Columbia (Forensic Psychiatric Institute), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 625, McLachlin J. (as she then was) explained the principles underlying the application of Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code as follows: In summary, the purpose of Part XX.1 is to replace the common law regime for the treatment of those who offend while mentally ill with a new approach emphasizing individualized assessment and the provision of opportunities for appropriate treatment. Under Part XX.1, the NCR accused is neither convicted nor acquitted. Instead, he or she is found not criminally responsible by reason of illness at the time of the offence. This is not a finding of dangerousness. It is rather a finding that triggers a balanced assessment of the offender’s possible dangerousness and of what treatment‑associated measures are required to offset it. Throughout the process the offender is to be treated with dignity and accorded the maximum liberty compatible with Part XX.1’s goals of public protection and fairness to the NCR accused. [Emphasis added; para. 43.]

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Part XX.1 applies to NCR accused, replacing common law regime with individualized assessment and treatment balancing protection and fairness.

propositions.text: The court will review s.16 Cr. C. conditions and then consider issues specific to toxic psychoses from self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: With these general considerations in mind, I will now review the conditions that must be met for s. 16 Cr. C. to apply in order to determine, in particular, whether those conditions are met in this case. After this review, I will consider issues related specifically to toxic psychoses that result from a state of self‑induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court will review s.16 conditions and then address toxic psychoses from self-induced intoxication.

propositions.text: s.16(2) Cr. C. presumes no mental disorder exempting criminal responsibility; accused must prove mental disorder on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: Section 16(2) Cr. C. provides that “[e]very person is presumed not to suffer from a mental disorder so as to be exempt from criminal responsibility”. An accused who seeks to avoid criminal responsibility on this ground must prove on a balance of probabilities that, at the material time, he or she was suffering from “a mental disorder that rendered the person incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of the act or omission or of knowing that it was wrong” (s. 16(1) Cr. C.).

propositions.text: Chaulk held burden on accused infringes but is a reasonable limit on presumption of innocence under s.11(d) Charter.
propositions.quote: In Chaulk, this Court held that imposing this burden of proof on the accused infringed the presumption of innocence guaranteed by s. 11 (d) of the Charter but that this was nonetheless a reasonable limit on that presumption in a free and democratic society.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.16 presumes no mental disorder; accused must prove it on balance of probabilities, a reasonable Charter limit per Chaulk.

propositions.text: The defence requires a two-stage test: characterize mental state, then determine incapacity to know act was wrong.
propositions.quote: An accused who wishes to successfully raise the defence of mental disorder must therefore meet the requirements of a two‑stage statutory test. The first stage involves characterizing the mental state of the accused. The key issue to be decided at trial at this stage is whether the accused was suffering from a mental disorder in the legal sense at the time of the alleged events. The second stage of the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. concerns the effects of the mental disorder. At this stage, it must be determined whether, owing to his or her mental condition, the accused was incapable of “knowing that [the act or omission] was wrong” (s. 16(1) Cr. C.).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the defence requires a two-stage test: mental disorder characterization and incapacity to know wrongfulness.

propositions.text: It is undisputed appellant was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at the material time.
propositions.quote: In the instant case, it is not in dispute that the appellant was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at the material time.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant was in serious psychotic condition and unaware of his actions at the time.
propositions.quote: The trial judge wrote that [translation] “[a]t the time the criminal acts were committed, the accused did not realize what he was doing and was in a serious psychotic condition; there is no real dispute about this” (para. 2).

propositions.text: The only issue is whether the psychosis resulted from a mental disorder under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the only issue in this appeal is whether the psychosis resulted from a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellant's incapacity to distinguish right from wrong is undisputed; issue is whether psychosis is a mental disorder under s.16.

propositions.text: Criminal Code defines mental disorder as a disease of the mind, but this is circular and courts must delineate the concept.
propositions.quote: The Criminal Code does not contain a precise definition of the “mental disorder” concept for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. Section 2 Cr. C. simply provides that the term “mental disorder” means “a disease of the mind” (“toute maladie mentale” in French). Because of the circular nature of this definition, the courts have had to gradually delineate this legal concept over time.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Criminal Code defines mental disorder circularly as disease of the mind, requiring courts to delineate the concept.

propositions.text: Cooper holds disease of the mind includes any illness impairing mind and its functioning.
propositions.quote: In Cooper, Dickson J. stated that the “disease of the mind” concept includes “any illness, disorder or abnormal condition which impairs the human mind and its functioning” (p. 1159).

propositions.text: Rabey states the concept is broad, including organic and functional disorders, curable or not, temporary or recurring.
propositions.quote: In Rabey, Dickson J. explained that “the concept is broad, embracing mental disorders of organic and functional origin, whether curable or incurable, temporary or not, recurring or non‑recurring” (p. 533).

propositions.text: Definition's inclusiveness reflects Parliament's wish to protect public from threats posed by persons with mental disorders.
propositions.quote: the inclusive nature of the definition of “mental disorder” can be explained in particular by Parliament’s wish to give the public a high level of protection from persons who could be a threat to others (J. Barrett and R. Shandler, Mental Disorder in Canadian Criminal Law (loose‑leaf), at p. 4‑12).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Cooper and Rabey for a broad disease of the mind concept, reflecting Parliament's public protection intent.

propositions.text: The mental disorder concept evolves with medical science and cannot be precisely defined or exhaustively listed.
propositions.quote: The “mental disorder” concept continues to evolve, which means that it can be adapted continually to advances in medical science (R. v. Simpson (1977), 35 C.C.C. (2d) 337 (Ont. C.A.)).

propositions.text: Rabey states the concept is not capable of precise definition and is flexible to apply to current or future medical recognized disorders.
propositions.quote: As Martin J.A., writing for the Ontario Court of Appeal, stated in R. v. Rabey (1977), 17 O.R. (2d) 1, this concept “is not capable of precise definition” (p. 12).

propositions.text: The concept must be compatible with policy considerations underlying s.16 defence and medical science.
propositions.quote: It is thus flexible enough to apply to any mental condition that, according to medical science in its current or future state, is indicative of a disorder that impairs the human mind or its functioning, and the recognition of which is compatible with the policy considerations that underlie the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the mental disorder concept evolves with medical science and must align with s.16 policy considerations.

propositions.text: Disease of the mind is a legal concept with a medical dimension decided by the trial judge, not the jury.
propositions.quote: whether a particular mental condition can be characterized as a “mental disorder” is a question of law to be decided by the trial judge

propositions.text: Psychiatrists describe mental condition medically; judge decides if it fits 'disease of the mind'.
propositions.quote: It is the function of the psychiatrist to describe the accused’s mental condition and how it is considered from the medical point of view. It is for the Judge to decide whether the condition described is comprehended by the term ‘disease of the mind’

propositions.text: If judge finds mental condition is a mental disorder, jury decides if accused suffered from it at offence time.
propositions.quote: If the judge finds as a matter of law that the mental condition of the accused is a “mental disorder”, it will ultimately be up to the jury to decide whether, on the facts, the accused was suffering from such a mental disorder at the time of the offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that 'disease of the mind' is a legal question for the judge, with psychiatrists providing medical description, and jury deciding factual suffering.

propositions.text: Trial judge is not bound by medical evidence as experts ignore policy aspects of s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: the trial judge is not bound by the medical evidence, since medical experts generally take no account of the policy component of the analysis required by s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Expert opinion on whether condition is a 'mental disorder' has little evidentiary value.
propositions.quote: an expert’s opinion on the legal issue of whether the mental condition of the accused constitutes a “mental disorder” within the meaning of the Criminal Code has “little or no evidentiary value”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the judge is not bound by medical evidence and expert opinion on legal mental disorder status has little evidentiary value.

propositions.text: Stone summarized roles: legal question of what is 'disease of the mind', mixed law and fact on condition, fact on whether accused suffered it.
propositions.quote: Taken alone, the question of what mental conditions are included in the term “disease of the mind” is a question of law. However, the trial judge must also determine whether the condition the accused claims to have suffered from satisfies the legal test for disease of the mind. This involves an assessment of the particular evidence in the case rather than a general principle of law and is thus a question of mixed law and fact. . . . The question of whether the accused actually suffered from a disease of the mind is a question of fact to be determined by the trier of fact.

paragraphs.summary: Stone held that 'disease of the mind' is a legal question, with mixed law and fact on condition, and fact on whether accused suffered it.

propositions.text: Central issue: whether toxic psychosis from single intoxication episode is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: The main issue is whether a toxic psychosis caused exclusively by a single episode of intoxication constitutes a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: It is common ground appellant was psychotic and unable to distinguish right from wrong.
propositions.quote: It is common ground that the appellant was in a psychotic condition that prevented him from distinguishing right from wrong.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the main issue is whether toxic psychosis from single intoxication is a 'mental disorder'; appellant was psychotic and impaired.

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis must always be a 'mental disorder' based on medical diagnosis alone.
propositions.quote: To argue that toxic psychosis must always be considered a “mental disorder” is to say that the legal characterization exercise under s. 16 Cr. C. depends exclusively on a medical diagnosis.

propositions.text: Appellant's argument conflicts with case law and cannot succeed; it would wrongly shift legal responsibility to experts.
propositions.quote: This argument conflicts directly with this Court’s consistent case law over the past three decades and cannot succeed. It would shift the responsibility for deciding whether the accused is guilty from the judge or jury to the expert.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellant's argument that toxic psychosis always qualifies as mental disorder, as it conflicts with case law and shifts responsibility to experts.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis is medically diagnosed but its causes vary widely and are not always precisely identified.
propositions.quote: medical science does not always identify the causes of toxic psychosis as precisely as is required in law. Although toxic psychosis is always related to exposure to a toxic substance, the circumstances in which it may arise can vary a great deal.

propositions.text: Case law shows toxic psychosis arises in diverse circumstances (citing multiple cases).
propositions.quote: This is readily apparent from a review of the case law on this point (see R. v. Oakley... R. v. Paul...)

paragraphs.summary: The court notes toxic psychosis causes vary widely and case law shows diverse circumstances of its occurrence.

propositions.text: Many factors contribute to substance-induced psychosis, including personality, stress, drug dependence, heavy use, and withdrawal.
propositions.quote: Many factors might contribute to a state of substance‑induced psychosis, including the fact that symptoms of a paranoid personality disorder are active...

propositions.text: Variations in psychological makeup and drug use affect toxic psychosis; quantity and toxicity matter.
propositions.quote: This diversity of circumstances can be attributed to variations in psychological makeup and psychological histories... The quantity and toxicity of the drugs taken also seem to have a significant effect in this regard.

propositions.text: Each case depends on its facts and cannot always fit existing case law easily.
propositions.quote: As a result, in each new situation, the case turns on its own facts and cannot always be fitted easily into the existing case law.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains many factors affect toxic psychosis and each case depends on its own facts, defying easy categorization.

propositions.text: It is unwise to adopt appellant's broad approach to toxic psychosis as always a mental disorder.
propositions.quote: Because of the heterogeneous nature of the circumstances... I consider it unwise to adopt an approach as broad as the one proposed by the appellant.

propositions.text: Cooper urges caution with intoxication-related mental conditions and recommends a contextual approach balancing public safety and criminal responsibility.
propositions.quote: In Cooper, this Court instead urged the courts to exercise particular caution where an accused person’s mental condition was closely related to an episode of intoxication contemporaneous with the offence.

propositions.text: Contextual approach requires case-specific analysis; toxic psychosis is not always a disease of the mind legally.
propositions.quote: Since this contextual approach means that a court must base its analysis on the particular circumstances of the case before it, I cannot accept the recent decisions or opinions that seem to suggest that toxic psychosis is always a disease of the mind

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellant's broad approach, endorses Cooper's contextual approach, and denies toxic psychosis is always a legal disease of the mind.

propositions.text: Court should start from presumption that temporary psychosis from intoxication is excluded under Cooper.
propositions.quote: a court should start from the general principle that temporary psychosis is covered by the exclusion from Cooper.

propositions.text: Accused can rebut presumption by showing disease of mind unrelated to intoxication symptoms.
propositions.quote: the accused can rebut the presumption provided for in s. 16(2) Cr. C. by showing that... he or she was suffering from a disease of the mind that was unrelated to the intoxication‑related symptoms.

propositions.text: Court should adopt Stone's 'more holistic approach' to determine if mental condition is a 'mental disorder'.
propositions.quote: the court should adopt the “more holistic approach” described by Bastarache J. in Stone (para. 203).

propositions.text: Attorney General of Ontario supports holistic approach to determine mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: As the Attorney General of Ontario suggested in this Court, it is ultimately this “more holistic approach” that will enable a court to determine whether the mental condition of an accused at the material time constitutes a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states courts should presume temporary psychosis from intoxication is excluded, but accused can rebut using Stone's holistic approach, supported by AG Ontario.

propositions.text: Stone proposes flexible approach with two analytical tools and policy considerations to distinguish mental conditions under s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: Bastarache J. proposed a flexible approach structured around two analytical tools and certain policy considerations.

propositions.text: Purpose is to distinguish mental conditions within s.16 Cr.C. from self-induced states excluded by Cooper.
propositions.quote: The purpose of the approach is to help the courts distinguish mental conditions that fall within the scope of s. 16 Cr. C. from those covered by Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs”

paragraphs.summary: Stone's flexible approach uses two analytical tools and policy considerations to distinguish mental disorders from self-induced states excluded by Cooper.

propositions.text: Internal cause factor compares accused to normal person to see if trigger is external or internal.
propositions.quote: the trial judge must consider the nature of the trigger and determine whether a normal person in the same circumstances might have reacted to it by entering an automatistic state as the accused claims to have done

propositions.text: If normal person might react similarly, trigger is external and excludes condition from s.16 Cr.C. mental disorder scope.
propositions.quote: The more the psychiatric evidence suggests that a normal person... is susceptible to such a state, the more justified the courts will be in finding that the trigger is external. Such a finding would exclude the condition of the accused from the scope of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Stone's internal cause factor compares accused to normal person; if normal person reacts similarly, trigger is external and excludes mental disorder under s.16.

propositions.text: Trigger can be alcohol or drugs; court must consider all circumstances of consumption in comparison to normal person.
propositions.quote: there is no reason why it cannot consist of alcohol or drug use contemporaneous with the offence... this comparison must take account of all the circumstances in which the accused consumed the drugs that triggered the psychotic condition.

propositions.text: If normal person might develop toxic psychosis from similar drug use, mental disorder is external and excluded from s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: If a normal person might also have reacted to similar drug use by developing toxic psychosis, it will be easier for the court to find that the mental disorder of the accused was purely external in origin... and was not a disease of the mind within the meaning of the Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains trigger can be drugs; if normal person might develop toxic psychosis similarly, mental disorder is external and excluded under s.16.

propositions.text: Continuing danger factor assesses likelihood of recurring danger to others to determine disease of the mind.
propositions.quote: The purpose of this factor is to assess the likelihood of recurring danger to others... the court must consider... the psychiatric history of the accused and the likelihood that the trigger alleged to have caused the automatistic episode will recur

paragraphs.summary: The continuing danger factor assesses likelihood of recurring danger to others to determine disease of the mind.

propositions.text: Recurring danger must arise independently of accused's will; voluntary future danger is not from mental disorder under s.16.
propositions.quote: danger will be recurring only if it is likely to arise again independently of the exercise of the will of the accused... a danger to public safety that might be voluntarily created by the accused in the future by consuming drugs would not be the result of a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Mental disorder defence exempts morally involuntary actions posing inherent danger despite accused's will.
propositions.quote: the effect of the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. is to exempt from criminal responsibility an accused whose actions are morally involuntary... the mental condition of the accused poses an inherent danger, that is, a danger that persists despite the will of the accused.

paragraphs.summary: The court states recurring danger must be independent of accused's will; voluntary future danger is not mental disorder under s.16 defence.

propositions.text: Holistic approach allows judges to consider policy concerns, mainly protecting society via Part XX.1 of Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: a holistic approach to disease of the mind must also permit trial judges to consider other policy concerns which underlie this inquiry... The main policy consideration continues to be the need to protect society from the accused through the special procedure set out in Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: If pre-existing condition poses no threat or need for treatment, court should more easily find no disease of the mind.
propositions.quote: if the circumstances of a case suggest that a pre‑existing condition of the accused does not require any particular treatment and is not a threat to others, the court should more easily hold that the accused was not suffering from a disease of the mind at the time of the alleged events.

paragraphs.summary: The holistic approach lets judges consider policy, mainly public protection; no threat or treatment need means no disease of the mind.

propositions.text: Contextual approach defines appeal scope; no exhaustive rule for all toxic psychosis cases.
propositions.quote: The purpose of the appeal is not to identify a rule to be applied to every case of toxic psychosis... it would be counterproductive to try to formulate an exhaustive definition of the mental conditions covered by Cooper’s exclusion

propositions.text: This case concerns toxic psychosis from a single episode of self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: The instant case concerns just one type of toxic psychosis, namely one that resulted exclusively from a single episode of self‑induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court limits appeal to toxic psychosis from single self-induced intoxication episode; no exhaustive rule for all cases.

propositions.text: Courts should do individualized analysis applying Stone's holistic approach to each toxic psychosis case.
propositions.quote: courts should determine on a case‑by‑case basis, applying the “more holistic approach” from Stone, whether the mental condition of each accused is included in or excluded from the definition of “disease of the mind”

propositions.text: This approach aligns with Rabey endorsing case-by-case decisions for transient mental disturbances.
propositions.quote: this approach is consistent with the line of authority based on Rabey, in which this Court endorsed Martin J.A.’s opinion that “[p]articular transient mental disturbances may not . . . be capable of being properly categorized... and must be decided on a case‑by‑case basis”

paragraphs.summary: The court endorses case-by-case analysis using Stone's holistic approach, consistent with Rabey's transient disturbance rulings.

propositions.text: Court will determine if appellant had mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C. using trial judge's findings.
propositions.quote: I must now determine whether the appellant was suffering from a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. at the material time... Judge Decoste found that the appellant... was in a psychotic condition caused by the voluntary consumption of drugs.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant's psychosis originated in drug use moments before offences.
propositions.quote: the psychotic condition the accused was in when he committed these criminal acts originated in his drug use during the moments leading up to them

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis is necessarily a mental disorder as an abnormal effect of intoxication affecting predisposed persons.
propositions.quote: appellant’s central argument is based on the contention that toxic psychosis is necessarily a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. because it is an “abnormal effect” of intoxication that affects only those who have a psychological predisposition or whose psyches are particularly fragile.

paragraphs.summary: The court will decide if appellant had mental disorder under s.16, noting trial judge found psychosis from drug use; appellant argues toxic psychosis is always a mental disorder.

propositions.text: Evidence does not support appellant's distinction between normal and abnormal intoxication effects or predisposition argument.
propositions.quote: The evidence in the record does not support the distinction drawn by the appellant between “normal effects” and “abnormal effects” of intoxication. Nor is it compatible with the argument that only persons who are predisposed to a mental disorder are likely to develop toxic psychosis as a result of drug use.

propositions.text: Dr. Faucher testified toxic psychosis cases occur weekly; 50% of PCP users likely develop psychosis when intoxicated.
propositions.quote: Dr. Faucher testified at trial that he saw cases of toxic psychosis “every week”... half (50 percent) of subjects who take drugs containing PCP are likely to develop a psychotic condition when intoxicated.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis is a frequent phenomenon resulting from high toxicity of chemical drugs.
propositions.quote: toxic psychosis is unfortunately a fairly frequent phenomenon that seems to result from the high toxicity of chemical drugs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence contradicts appellant's distinction and predisposition claim; toxic psychosis is frequent from toxic drugs.

propositions.text: Stone's first factor suggests a normal person would develop toxic psychosis from one 'poire bleue' pill, contradicting appellant.
propositions.quote: The application of the first factor from Stone thus suggests that the taking of one “poire bleue” pill is a specific external factor that contradicts the appellant’s argument, since it seems likely that the reaction of a normal person to such a pill would indeed be to develop toxic psychosis.

propositions.text: This suggests appellant was not suffering from a mental disorder at the time of the acts.
propositions.quote: This strongly suggests that the appellant was not suffering from a mental disorder at the time he committed the impugned acts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Stone's first factor shows a normal person would develop toxic psychosis from the pill, suggesting appellant lacked a mental disorder.

propositions.text: Rapid psychotic symptoms indicate delusions are due to an external factor, here self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: The rapid appearance of psychotic symptoms generally indicates that the delusions of the accused can be attributed to a specific external factor.

propositions.text: Dr. Faucher's assessment shows rapid symptom reversal is characteristic of toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: Dr. Faucher’s expert assessment, which the trial judge preferred to that of Dr. Turmel, an expert called by the defence, revealed that the rapid reversal of symptoms is characteristic of a toxic psychosis caused by an episode of self‑induced intoxication

propositions.text: Professor Parent states delusions subsiding with drug effects indicate substance intoxication, not disease of the mind under Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: delusions that subside at the same rate as the drug are usually signs of Substance Intoxication

propositions.text: Such delusions do not result from a disease of the mind within the meaning of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: Such delusions therefore do not result from a disease of the mind within the meaning of the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds rapid psychotic symptoms and their reversal indicate toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication, not a disease of the mind under the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Appellant's psychotic symptoms diminished after taking the drug and disappeared by October 28, 2005.
propositions.quote: the psychotic symptoms experienced by the appellant began to diminish shortly after he took the “poire bleue” pill and continued to do so until they disappeared completely on October 28, 2005.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held symptoms coincided with intoxication duration; appellant was sane after drug effects passed.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal held that the disappearance of the symptoms showed that the symptoms of toxic psychosis coincided with the duration of the appellant’s intoxication.

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. stated appellant had no disease of the mind before crimes and was sane after drug effects ended.
propositions.quote: Thibault J.A. could thus say that “[t]he appellant suffered from no [disease of the mind] before committing the crimes, and once the effects of the drug consumption had passed, he was entirely sane”

propositions.text: Court sees no valid reason to depart from Court of Appeal's conclusion on appellant's sanity post-intoxication.
propositions.quote: I see no valid reason to depart from this conclusion.
