paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the Court of Appeal that appellant's psychotic symptoms matched intoxication duration and he was sane after drug effects ended.

propositions.text: No evidence shows appellant's mental condition is inherently dangerous if he abstains from drugs voluntarily.
propositions.quote: there is no evidence indicating that the mental condition of the accused is inherently dangerous in any way. Provided that the appellant abstains from such drugs in the future, which he is capable of doing voluntarily, it would seem that his mental condition poses no threat to public safety.

propositions.text: Whether appellant's drug dependency affects his ability to abstain and thus poses a recurring danger.
propositions.quote: Although I will not adopt a definitive position on this question, I might have concluded otherwise if the appellant had a dependency on drugs that affected his ability to stop using them voluntarily.

propositions.text: If appellant had drug dependency impairing voluntary abstinence, risk of recurring danger might be greater.
propositions.quote: The likelihood of recurring danger might then be greater.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence appellant's mental condition is dangerous if he abstains voluntarily, but notes dependency could increase risk.

propositions.text: No valid reason to initiate special procedure under Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code for appellant's condition.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that there is no valid reason to initiate the special procedure provided for in Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: An accused with mental condition solely from temporary self-induced intoxication and no threat to others is not suffering from a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr.
propositions.quote: An accused whose mental condition at the material time can be attributed exclusively to a state of temporary self‑induced intoxication and who poses no threat to others is not suffering from a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Part XX.1 applies only if accused actually suffered from a disease of the mind at the material time, not temporary intoxication-induced madness.
propositions.quote: The scheme of Part XX.1 applies only if the accused actually suffered from a disease of the mind at the material time. It is not intended to apply to accused persons whose temporary madness was induced artificially by a state of intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Part XX.1 does not apply to temporary self-induced intoxication without threat, as it requires actual disease of the mind.

propositions.text: Appellant was not suffering from a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. at the time of the assault.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the appellant was not suffering from a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. at the time he committed the assault.

propositions.text: Appellant failed to rebut presumption that toxic psychosis was self-induced by alcohol or drugs per Cooper definition.
propositions.quote: He has failed to rebut the presumption that his toxic psychosis was a “self‑induced stat[e] caused by alcohol or drugs” in accordance with the definition in Cooper.

propositions.text: Malfunctioning mind from self-induced intoxication is not a legal disease of the mind as it is not inherent psychological makeup.
propositions.quote: A malfunctioning of the mind that results exclusively from self‑induced intoxication cannot be considered a disease of the mind in the legal sense, since it is not a product of the individual’s inherent psychological makeup.

propositions.text: Medical science may consider such conditions diseases of the mind, but legally toxic psychosis is a symptom of self-induced intoxication state.
propositions.quote: This is true even though medical science may tend to consider such conditions to be diseases of the mind. In circumstances like those of the case at bar, toxic psychosis seems to be nothing more than a symptom, albeit an extreme one, of the accused person’s state of self‑induced intoxication.

propositions.text: Such a state cannot justify exempting accused from criminal responsibility under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: Such a state cannot justify exempting an accused from criminal responsibility under s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes appellant's toxic psychosis was self-induced and not a legal mental disorder, so no exemption from criminal responsibility applies.

propositions.text: Policy considerations from Cooper support excluding self-induced intoxication states from s.16 Cr. C. defence.
propositions.quote: This conclusion takes account of the policy considerations referred to by Dickson J. in Cooper.

propositions.text: Dr. Faucher's expert assessment shows toxic psychosis frequency in similar cases.
propositions.quote: In light of Dr. Faucher’s expert assessment of the frequency of toxic psychosis in circumstances analogous to the ones in the instant case,

propositions.text: Appellant's position would broaden s.16 defence scope beyond Parliament's intent if accepted.
propositions.quote: the appellant’s position, if adopted, would affect the integrity of the criminal justice system in ways that would be difficult to accept.

propositions.text: If all violent offenders with toxic psychosis were found not criminally responsible, s.16 defence would be broader than intended.
propositions.quote: If everyone who committed a violent offence while suffering from toxic psychosis were to be found not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder regardless of the origin or cause of the psychosis, the scope of the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. would become much broader than Parliament intended.

propositions.text: These considerations reinforce that appellant's toxic psychosis is excluded from s.16 defence as self-induced state per Cooper.
propositions.quote: These considerations reinforce the conclusion that the toxic psychosis of the appellant in this case is covered by Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs”.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds policy and expert evidence support excluding self-induced toxic psychosis from s.16 defence to preserve criminal justice integrity.

propositions.text: No evidence appellant had underlying mental disorder simplifies legal characterization under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: The lack of evidence that the appellant was suffering from an underlying mental disorder certainly simplifies the legal characterization exercise under s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: This case is clear: appellant's mental condition falls under Cooper's exclusion for self-induced states.
propositions.quote: From a factual standpoint, this case seems quite clear: as in Paul, the only reasonable conclusion is that the appellant’s mental condition is covered by the exclusion from Cooper.

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis was caused by underlying mental disorder, not self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: Contrary to the conclusion the appellant is asking this Court to draw, it would be unreasonable to assume, absent any evidence to back up such a claim, that the real cause of his toxic psychosis was an underlying mental disorder.

propositions.text: No Canadian court has applied s.16 defence for toxic psychosis without evidence of underlying disease of the mind.
propositions.quote: In addition, no Canadian court has applied the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. in the context of toxic psychosis without evidence showing that the accused suffered from an underlying disease of the mind.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of underlying mental disorder and rejects appellant's claim, noting no precedent applying s.16 defence without such evidence.

propositions.text: Courts will face harder cases where mental disorder and drug-induced psychosis coexist.
propositions.quote: it is plausible to expect that the courts will have to perform this legal characterization exercise in circumstances much more difficult than the ones in the case at bar.

propositions.text: Example: mental disorder present but toxic psychosis triggered by drug use that could affect normal person similarly.
propositions.quote: One example would be a case in which the mental condition of the accused indicates an underlying mental disorder but the evidence also shows that the toxic psychosis was triggered by the consumption of drugs of a nature and in a quantity that could have produced the same condition in a normal person.

propositions.text: In such cases, courts should apply Stone's 'more holistic approach' carefully.
propositions.quote: In such circumstances, the courts should be especially meticulous in applying the “more holistic approach” from Stone.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes future cases with mixed mental disorder and drug-induced psychosis require careful application of Stone's holistic approach.

propositions.text: Whether s.33.1 Cr. C. applies given intoxication and conduct at material time.
propositions.quote: The foregoing conclusion leads to the question whether s. 33.1 Cr. C. is applicable.

propositions.text: s.33.1 Cr. C. applies if accused was intoxicated, intoxication self-induced, and accused departed from reasonable care by interfering with another's bodily integrity.
propositions.quote: This provision applies where three conditions are met: (1) the accused was intoxicated at the material time; (2) the intoxication was self‑induced; and (3) the accused departed from the standard of reasonable care generally recognized in Canadian society by interfering or threatening to interfere with the bodily integrity of another person

propositions.text: Cases R. v. Vickberg and R. v. Chaulk illustrate s.33.1 Cr. C. application.
propositions.quote: see, generally, R. v. Vickberg (1998), 16 C.R. (5th) 164 (B.C.S.C.); R. v. Chaulk, 2007 NSCA 84, 257 N.S.R. (2d) 99

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.33.1 Cr. C. applies if accused was self-intoxicated and breached reasonable care by threatening bodily integrity.

propositions.text: Self-induced intoxication under s.33.1 Cr. C. is limited to period substance effects last.
propositions.quote: The self‑induced intoxication to which s. 33.1 Cr. C. refers is limited in time. It corresponds to the period during which the substance consumed by the accused produced its effects.

propositions.text: s.33.1(2) Cr. C. states person is criminally at fault if in self-induced intoxication state and interferes with another's bodily integrity.
propositions.quote: It provides that a person “is . . . criminally at fault where the person, while in a state of self‑induced intoxication that renders the person unaware of, or incapable of consciously controlling, their behaviour, voluntarily or involuntarily interferes or threatens to interfere with the bodily integrity of another person”.

propositions.text: s.33.1 Cr. C. prevents accused avoiding liability by claiming intoxication negated intent or voluntariness.
propositions.quote: Section 33.1 Cr. C. is intended to prevent an accused from avoiding criminal liability on the ground that his or her state of intoxication at the material time rendered the accused incapable of forming the mental element or having the voluntariness required to commit the offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.33.1 Cr. C. covers self-induced intoxication during substance effects and prevents intoxication defence to criminal liability.

propositions.text: s.33.1 Cr. C. applies to any mental condition directly from intoxication, including toxic psychosis.
propositions.quote: Section 33.1 Cr. C. therefore applies to any mental condition that is a direct extension of a state of intoxication.

propositions.text: Appellant wrongly suggests s.33.1 Cr. C. applies only to 'normal effects' of intoxication.
propositions.quote: The appellant’s suggestion that it applies only to the “normal effects” of intoxication is wrong.

propositions.text: No intoxication threshold excludes s.33.1 Cr. C.; toxic psychosis is covered by it.
propositions.quote: There is no threshold of intoxication beyond which s. 33.1 Cr. C. does not apply to an accused, which means that toxic psychosis can be one of the states of intoxication covered by this provision.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis is covered by s.33.1 Cr. C. in this case; Court of Appeal correctly held s.33.1 applies, not s.16.
propositions.quote: It is so covered in the case at bar. The Court of Appeal therefore did not err in law in holding that s. 33.1 Cr. C. was applicable rather than s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds s.33.1 Cr. C. applies to toxic psychosis and rejects appellant's narrow interpretation, affirming Court of Appeal's ruling.

propositions.text: Appeal is dismissed for all reasons stated.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, the appeal must be dismissed. Appeal dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal.
